country.comment: Study examines the 2016 water crisis on San Andres Island, in the Archipelago of San Andres, Providencia and Santa Catalina, Colombia.
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF p. 3, Introduction; PDF p. 5, Case presentation

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative case study; descriptive secondary/administrative figures (e.g., >14,000 people affected, 31.6%-36.7% or 35% aqueduct coverage across 14,841 households, >18 million liters emergency tanker water distributed) provide context rather than inferential quantitative effect estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Institutional response to the 2016 San Andres water crisis relied on a conservative, technocratic, supply-side approach shaped in closed-door sessions with the private concessionaire Proactiva/Veolia, dividing affected residents into formal aqueduct subscribers and non-subscribers (with piped coverage reaching only 31.6%–36.7% of the population / 35% of 14,841 households). Under the 2005 concession contract, northern tourist areas received piped water 24 hours/day whereas poor and Raizal sectors received water once every 20 days, and during the 2016 crisis (affecting more than 14,000 people) Veolia restricted piped delivery to subscribers while selling water to the government for rationed emergency tanker distribution to non-subscribers. Despite State of Public Calamity Decree 0170 of 2016, delayed desalination plant procurement, and late-2018 contract amendment 'Otro Si No. 9' extending Veolia's operation for another 15 years, November 2018 interviews showed no structural change in water access for non-connected and southern/hilly Raizal and low-income neighborhoods, where residents still received piped water only once per month or experienced month-long outages and recurring protests.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF pp. 8-9, Case presentation; PDF pp. 18, 20-24, Results; PDF pp. 26-28, Conclusions

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 2 (mechanism directly observed) and capped at 2 by qualitative design ceiling per CODEBOOK.md §9. Interviews with Veolia personnel, local officials, and residents together with concession and emergency decrees directly document how contractual subscriber restrictions, differentiated supply schedules (24h/day vs once every 20 days), closed-door technocratic decision-making, operator contract disputes/delays, and ad hoc tanker rationing governed unequal water access.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 8-9, Case presentation; PDF pp. 16-24, Results; PDF pp. 26-28, Conclusions

mechanism_flags.comment: Covers ELIGIBILITY (service_area division between aqueduct subscribers in northern/tourist districts and excluded non-subscribers in southern/western/rural areas under the 2005 concession and 2018 'Otro Si No. 9' extension; technocratic supply-side infrastructure and land/water planning), BURDEN (multi-year administrative and contractual delay in procuring/operating promised desalination plants and unfulfilled 2016 protest agreements), and DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION (discretionary emergency tanker routing, rationing, and irregular tank refilling; ad hoc emergency water trucking and communal tanks under Public Calamity Decree 0170 of 2016 as temporary accommodation; exclusion of community/Raizal leaders from closed-door crisis response vs protest-driven participation; institutional_fragmentation and unclear drought competences across agencies; political_coordination via the State Council for Risk Management and local-national/utility negotiations).

outcome_flags.comment: Examines household water_access across 2016 and 2018, formal_connection (aqueduct subscribers vs non-subscribers and prioritized connection of two neighborhoods), service_coverage (31.6%-36.7% / 35% of 14,841 households), service_continuity and service_reliability (24h/day supply in the north vs once every 20 days or once/month and 1-4 month outages in hilly/south sectors), service_quantity (1,500-2,000 L/family emergency rations and tourist vs local consumption), service_quality (aquifer salinity and low water quality in 93% of analyzed wells), and affordability (high cost of commercial water trucks and inability of poorer households to afford cisterns).
